    AI Overview
    The 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967 following JFK’s assassination, dictates presidential succession and procedures for handling presidential incapacity
    . It ensures continuous leadership if a president dies, resigns, or is incapacitated, allowing the Vice President to become president or Acting President. It also allows for filling VP vacancies. 
    Key Sections of the 25th Amendment 
    • Section 1 (Succession): If the President dies, resigns, or is removed, the Vice President becomes President.
    • Section 2 (VP Vacancy): If the Vice Presidency is vacant, the President nominates a replacement, confirmed by a majority vote in both Houses of Congress.
    • Section 3 (Voluntary Transfer):
      The President may declare in writing they are unable to perform duties, making the VP Acting President until a written declaration to the contrary is sent.
    • Section 4 (Involuntary Transfer): The VP and a majority of the Cabinet (or other body authorized by Congress) can declare the President unable to discharge duties. The VP immediately assumes duties as Acting President. 
    Purpose and Benefits 
    • Continuity of Government: Addresses both temporary and permanent disability, eliminating ambiguity that existed prior to 1967.
    • Ensures Stability: Provides a clear, legal framework for transferring power in a crisis, avoiding power vacuums. 
    Notable Applications 
    • Filling Vice Presidential Vacancies: Used in 1973 when Gerald Ford replaced Spiro Agnew, and in 1974 when Nelson Rockefeller filled the vacancy left by Ford.
    • Presidential Incapacity (Temporary): Used by President Reagan in 1985 (during surgery) and President George W. Bush in 2002 and 2007 (during procedures).
    • Section 4 Discussions: Although Section 4 has never been fully invoked to remove a president against their will, it has been discussed in cases of potential presidential incapacity.
